title: The Kohler Effect
text:
In the 1920s, the German psychologist Otto Kohler studied members of a rowing club doing a strength endurance exercise, curling a weight as many times as they could. He compared how long they lasted alone and in pairs, where the pair's result ended as soon as the weaker member gave up. He found that in some pairs, the weaker member lasted longer than he had alone, especially when the two partners differed moderately in ability.

For decades the finding was largely forgotten, overshadowed by research on social loafing. In 2000, Guido Hertel, Norbert Kerr and Lawrence Messe revived it in a series of experiments with modern controls.

Participants performed physically tiring persistence tasks, alone and in two-person teams. In some conditions, the team's score depended on the weaker member's performance, so that member was indispensable. These were compared with conditions in which the two members' scores were simply added together.

When the team's result depended on the weaker member, that person persisted noticeably longer than they did alone. This motivation gain, which the authors named the Kohler effect, was linked to the weaker member's sense that their effort was indispensable to the team and to comparisons with the more capable partner.
lesson: Being the weak link that the team depends on can bring out extra effort. Pair people with slightly stronger partners on tasks where each person's part truly counts.
people: Guido Hertel, Norbert Kerr, Lawrence Messe; Otto Kohler
source: Hertel, G., Kerr, N. L., and Messe, L. A. (2000). Motivation gains in performance groups: Paradigmatic and theoretical developments on the Kohler effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(4), 580-601.
